title: Co-fermented Coffee
description: Co-fermented coffee is fermented with something else in the tank: fruit, cacao, sometimes a chosen yeast. It is not the same as a washed coffee, a natural, or a bean that has simply been flavoured.
author: Keiran Jones
excerpt: Co-fermented coffee is fermented with something else in the tank: fruit, cacao, sometimes a chosen yeast. It is not the same as a washed coffee, a natural, or a bean that has simply been flavoured.
body:
Co-fermented coffee is a coffee that has been fermented with something else in the tank. Fruit, fruit pulp, cacao, cane, sometimes a chosen yeast. The extra ingredient is there while the microbes are working, which is the whole point of it. It is not the same thing as [washing](/archive/coffee-processing-methods-from-cherry-to-green-bean) the mucilage off, and it is not the same thing as drying the cherry whole.

A normal fermentation is already part of washed and [honey](/archive/coffee-processing-the-honey-process) coffee. Yeasts and bacteria eat the sugars in the mucilage, and that changes the cup. A [natural](/archive/the-dry-process-an-introduction-to-natural-coffees) goes further, because the whole cherry is dried and the fruit stays in contact with the seed for weeks. Co-fermentation takes that idea and adds another food on purpose. Passion fruit, peach, watermelon, cacao pulp. The hope is a cup where you can taste that ingredient as well as the coffee.

## Why there are so many of them

[Colombia](/country-guide-colombia) is where a lot of people meet these coffees. [Perfect Daily Grind](https://perfectdailygrind.com/2026/02/why-colombia-produces-co-fermented-coffees/) has written about why. Farmers are under pressure from costs and from prices that jump around, and a co-ferment can sell for more than a clean washed regional. Some of the fruit ferments began as a way to use fruit that could not be exported. The volumes are still small next to washed Colombia. They are not about to replace the milds the country is known for, and they should not be asked to.

Other countries do it too. Panama, Costa Rica and Brazil have their own versions. Colombia is just the one you see most often on a specialty menu at the moment, partly because there are a lot of farmers who already know how to ferment carefully, and partly because buyers will pay for a cup that tastes like a named fruit.

The extra fruit also makes the process fussier. There is more sugar in the tank, the fermentation runs faster, and it is easier to spoil a lot. That is why the good ones cost what they cost. You are paying for the fruit and for someone standing over the tank.

## A co-ferment is not an infused coffee

This is the bit worth being fussy about. A co-ferment is supposed to be a fermentation. An infused coffee can mean something much blunter: flavourings added so the green bean soaks them up, with no need for a fermentation at all.

[Perfect Daily Grind put the difference plainly](https://perfectdailygrind.com/2024/10/why-infused-co-fermented-coffees-are-different/). For a co-ferment or a controlled fermentation, yeasts and bacteria have to consume compounds in the coffee and make new ones. For an infusion, you can add synthetic chemicals and flavourings. The bean absorbs them. Some people use the two words as if they were the same. They are not, and the bag should not pretend they are.

You can taste it when the process has gone wrong. A careful lot still tastes like coffee, with the fruit sitting in the cup rather than replacing it. A clumsy one tastes like fruit juice, or like a flavouring. 'Fruit bomb' has become both the compliment and the warning.

## Synthetic flavours

There are reports that some coffees sold into this craze have had synthetic flavourings added to the green coffee. Pergamino, working with researchers at Universidad Surcolombiana, said that [all 25 co-fermented samples they tested contained propylene glycol](https://www.facebook.com/pergaminocafe/posts/we-wanted-to-share-with-the-level-of-detail-and-rigor-that-matters-to-us-why-we-/1030649949311590/), a carrier used in flavourings. That is one set of samples, not every co-ferment on earth. It is still a reason to ask what went into the tank.

Flavour chemist Ennio Cantergiani has [published GC-MS work](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ennio-cantergiani-36808a1_stop-laundering-flavoured-coffee-as-experimental-activity-7408855102842671106-4hjK) on coffees marketed as co-ferments that turned up the same kind of fingerprint: propylene glycol, and flavour molecules used in formulated flavourings rather than in a fruit ferment. Fermented watermelon should taste fermented. A fresh, sweet-shop watermelon note is a different kind of addition.

None of that means a named fruit in a fermentation tank is a trick. It means the word co-ferment is being asked to cover two different products, and only one of them is a fermentation.

## How to drink one

Treat it as its own drink. Brew it the way you would a juicy natural, a little cooler than a dense washed coffee, and leave the milk out if you want to know what you bought. If you can, taste it next to a washed coffee from the same region. Colombia still has plenty of those, and they are the reason the origin has the reputation it does. A co-ferment is an extra, not a replacement.

If the roaster will not say what was added, I would leave it. The interesting ones are proud of the recipe.
seoDescription: What co-fermented coffee is, how it differs from a washed, natural or infused coffee, and why some fruit-bomb lots are being questioned.
